Materials and methods
Ethics statement
All experiments involving animals were conducted according to the ethical policies and procedures approved by the Boston Children’s Hospital’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol 0001619) and followed the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (NIH Publication 8523, revised 2011) and the ARVO Statement for Use of Animals in Ophthalmic Vision and Research.
Mice
Acox1
heterozygous mice
[37]
were cryo-recovered (029747, Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME, USA) and bred generating global KO mice, wild type (WT) littermate controls, and heterozygous breeders. Female and male mice were used for experiments. Transnetyx, Inc. (Cordova, TN, USA) assessed genotypes.
In mice, retinal neuron differentiation concludes within the first 2 weeks after birth, while synapse formation is completed around postnatal day (P) 20
[38]
,
[39]
. At P30, conducting ERG starts getting feasible. The retina continues maturing with increasing ERG amplitude from 1 to 2 months of age
[40]
. We therefore performed ERG on P30 and P60 to study developmental retinal function during nutrient interventions. Pyruvate was chosen because it was minimally detected in
Acox1
KO retinas. DHA was significantly decreased in
Acox1
KO retinas according to fatty acid profiling. Clinical trials of DHA supplementation in premature infants demonstrate that DHA and ARA at a 1:2 ratio exerts protection against retinopathy
[41]
,
[42]
. Therefore, we included combined diet with DHA:ARA at 1:2 ratio in addition to DHA alone to test which diet would exert better protection against retinal defects caused by the loss of
Acox1
. For pyruvate intervention,
Acox1
KO mice were intraperitoneally injected with pyruvate at a dose of 50 µg/g body weight, as previously reported
[43]
, or vehicle phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) daily from P30-P60. For dietary lipid supplementation,
Acox1
KO mice were fed completely defined rodent feed (Research Diets, Inc., New Brunswick, NJ, USA) containing either 3 % DHA or 1 % DHA plus 2 % arachidonic acid (ARA) of the diet’s total lipid composition (10 %) from P30-P60 (
Table 1
). DHA and ARA oils were obtained from DSM (Heerlen, Netherlands).

Electroretinography (ERG)
To assess retinal function in
Acox1
KO vs. WT mice, ERG was conducted at P30 when first feasible to perform
[44]
,
[45]
,
[46]
. Mice were dark-adapted, mydriatic, and anesthetized. Rod-mediated ERG was obtained using an Espion E
2
(Diagnosys LLC, Lowell, MA, USA). Stimuli were “green” light-emitting diode flashes of doubling intensity from ∼ 0.00025 to ∼ 2.05 cd⋅s/m
2
followed by “white” xenon-arc flashes from ∼ 8.2 to ∼ 1,050 cd⋅s/m
2
presented in an integrating sphere (Colordome, Diagnosys LLC). For light-adapted ERG, stimuli were “white” xenon-arc flashes ∼ 1.0 to 525 cd⋅s/m
2
. The amplitude and sensitivity of cone bipolar cells was estimated from
b
-waves.
For
Acox1
KO mice with nutrient intervention, flash ERGs were obtained using a Celeris High Throughput Testing System (Diagnosys LLC). Stimuli were “red” and “green” light-emitting diode flashes of doubling intensity from ∼ 0.00125 to ∼ 65.536 cd⋅s/m
2
.
The saturating amplitude and sensitivity of rod photoreceptors and second-order neurons, principally bipolar cells (
Fig. 1
A
), were estimated as reported
[47]
,
[48]
,
[49]
,
[50]
. All ERG data are presented as decimal logarithmic change from control (ΔLogControl) to obtain linear changes in observations of fixed proportion, consistent with a constant fraction for physiologically meaningful changes in parameter values
[51]
.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of the retina
Spectral-domain OCT under the guidance of bright-field live fundus imaging (Micron IV, Phoenix Research Laboratories, Pleasanton, CA, USA)
[44]
,
[46]
, was performed in
Acox1
KO vs. WT mice at P30 when retinal OCT first became feasible. Retinal thickness was measured using InSight software (Phoenix Research Laboratories). The total retinal thickness (inner limiting membrane to photoreceptor inner/outer segment layer) was plotted at 6 nasal and temporal distances (50, 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300 µm) from the optic nerve head
[44]
,
[46]
.
Immunohistochemistry
Immunohistochemistry was performed as described
[46]
,
[52]
. P30
Acox1
KO vs. WT eye cross sections containing the optic nerve head were treated with ice-cold methanol (room temperature (RT), 10 min) and 0.1 % Triton PBS (RT, 30 min) followed by blocking with 3 % bovine serum albumin (BSA) in 0.1 % Triton PBS (RT, 1 h) and staining with primary antibodies against rhodopsin (1:500, MABN15, Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA) and cone arrestin (1:500, AB15282, Millipore) (4°C, overnight). After incubation of corresponding fluorescent secondary antibodies (RT, 1 h), sections were covered in mounting medium with 4′,6-diamidine-2′-phenylindole dihydrochloride (DAPI, H-1200, Vector Laboratories, Newark, CA, USA). Images (200x magnification) were taken using a Zeiss confocal microscope (Oberkochen, Germany).
Transmission electron microscopy
Transmission electron microscopy was conducted as previously outlined with slight modifications
[53]
. In brief, mouse eyeballs were fixed overnight in ice-cold 2.5 % glutaraldehyde, 1.25 % formaldehyde, and 0.03 % picric acid in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.4). After washing with 0.1 M cacodylate buffer, the eyeballs were cut in half and osmicated in 1 % osmium tetroxide and 1.5 % potassium ferrocyanide for 3 h, followed by several washes in distilled H
2
O. Samples were then washed with maleate buffer and incubated with 1 % uranyl acetate in maleate buffer for 1 h and rinsed multiple times with maleate buffer (pH 5.2). Dehydration was carried out sequentially with a graded ethanol series (up to 100 %) at 4 °C, which was changed three times over the course of 1 h. The samples were then incubated in propylene oxide for 1 h. Subsequently, the samples were placed in a mixture of propylene oxide and TAAB resin (TAAB Laboratories Equipment Ltd, Berkshire, England) at a 1:1 ratio, including catalyst, and left overnight at 4 °C. The next day, the eyeballs were embedded in pure TAAB resin and polymerized at 60 °C for 48 h in an experimental oven. Resin blocks were gently trimmed and sectioned to a thickness of 80 nm using an Ultracut-S microtome (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany). The ultra-thin sections were placed onto formvar-carbon coated slot copper grids and stained with 0.2 % lead citrate. Processed samples were observed under a JEOL 1200x electron microscope (JEOL, Tokyo, Japan), and images were captured with an AMT 2k CCD camera (AMT, Boston, MA, USA) and stored as TIFF files.
Mitochondrial DNA copy number
The ratio of mitochondrial to nuclear DNA copy number (mtDNA/nDNA) of
Acox1
KO vs. WT retinas at P30 was assessed as described previously
[43]
.
Reverse transcription-quantitative PCR
Retinas from
Acox1
KO (with and without nutrient intervention) and WT mice were used for cDNA synthesis as reported
[44]
,
[45]
. PCR was performed for rhodopsin (
Rho
): 5′–TCATGGTCTTCGGAGGATTCAC–3′, 5′–TCACCTCCAAGTGTGGCAAAG–3′;
Gnat1
: 5′–AGTATGGAGATTCAGCCCGG–3′, 5′–GGTATTCTGAGGCTCGGTCA–3′;
Pde6b
: 5′–CCCCTGACTCTGAGATCGTC–3′, 5′–TGATCACAGCCACGACATCT–3′;
Pde6g
: 5′–CAGCCTGACAGAGTCCAGAA–3′, 5′–GCTTGCTCTTGAACTGCCTT–3′. Quantitative gene expression analysis was carried out through an Applied Biosystems 7300 Sequence Detection System (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and SYBR Green Master mix kit (Bimake.com, Huissen, Netherlands). Gene expression was normalized to cyclophilin A (5′-CAGACGCCACTGTCGCTTT-3′, 5′–TGTCTTTGGAACTTTGTCTGCAA-3′) using the ΔΔCt method.
Western blot
ACOX1 levels were assessed in protein lysates from P30
Acox1
KO vs. WT retinas using anti-ACOX1 antibody (1:1000,
AB184032
, Abcam, Cambridge, UK) in 5 % BSA (4 °C, overnight). Signals were detected using 1:10000 corresponding horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies and enhanced chemiluminescence (Pierce
TM
, Thermo Fisher Scientific) followed by imaging (Azure 600 Imaging System, Dublin, CA, USA)
[44]
. Anti-actin beta (1:2500, A1978, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) served as internal control.
Proteomics
Retinas from P30
Acox1
KO vs. WT mice (n = 6/group; both retinas pooled) were processed for label-free LC-MS/MS proteomics as described
[54]
. Mass spectrometry was performed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos coupled to an Easy-nLC1000 HPLC pump (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptide spectra were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer (version 2.5, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Proteins with ≥ 2 unique peptides were included
[54]
. Qlucore Omics Explorer (version 3.5, Qlucore, Lund, Sweden) was used for logarithmic transformation followed by student’s
t
-test (p-value) and Benjamini-Hochberg method correcting for multiple hypothesis testing (FDR-adjusted p-value, called q-value) for each protein. Significantly increased or decreased proteins (p < 0.05; q < 0.20) were analyzed for Gene Ontology (GO) pathway enrichment of Biological Process, Molecular Function, and Cellular Component using EnrichR (retrieved: September 2023)
[55]
,
[56]
,
[57]
. Fisher's exact test provided p-values, Benjamini-Hochberg method (correcting for multiple hypothesis testing) yielded q-values. Pathways with q < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched.
Raw data are available on the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE
[58]
repository (identifier PXD055240,
https://doi.org/10.6019/PXD055240)
.
Metabolomics
Retinas from P30
Acox1
KO vs. WT mice (n = 3 samples/group; 8 retinas pooled/sample) were processed by the NYU Metabolomics Core Resource Laboratory, New York, NY, USA. Metabolite extraction was carried out as previously described
[59]
. For polar untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics, a Waters
TM
Atlantis Premier Beh Z-HILIC Column, 1.7 µm, 2.1 mm x 150 mm (Waters Corporation, Milford, MA, USA) was coupled to a Dionex Ultimate 3000
TM
system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For MS analyses, the LC system was coupled to a Thermo Q Exactive HF
TM
mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Parameters were set, and relative quantification of metabolites was performed as reported
[59]
. When a metabolite’s peak intensity in a sample was below the blank threshold, the threshold value was imputed for statistical comparison. Student’s
t
-test was applied to generate p-values without correction for multiple hypothesis testing. Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05.
Raw data are deposited at Metabolomics Workbench (study_id:ST003533, datatrack_id:5226, http://dx.
https://doi.org/10.21228/M8MC1N)
[60]
.
Fatty acid profiling
Retinal samples from P30
Acox1
KO (n = 18; both retinas pooled) vs. WT mice (n = 17) were processed for total lipid extraction
[61]
. Retinas were weighed and homogenized by glass homogenizers with sequential addition of 1.75 mL 0.88 % potassium chloride, 2 mL methanol, and 4 mL chloroform. Heptadecanoic acid (17:0) served as internal standard. Total lipids were extracted overnight then methylated with methanolic boron trifluoride (100 °C, 1 h). Fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) were quantified with a gas chromatograph equipped with flame ionization detector (Varian, Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA). FAMEs were eluted on a DB-FFAP (30 m x 0.25 mm i.d. x 0.25 μm film thickness) column by set program at initial oven temperature of 50 °C for 1 min, following a ramp to 130 °C at a rate of 30 °C/min, 175 °C at 10 °C/min, 230 °C at 5 °C/min then held for 9.5 min, and a ramp to 240 °C at 5 °C/min for 11.13 min. Via peak comparison to internal standard, 31 fatty acid species were quantified (8 species of saturated and 8 species of monounsaturated fatty acids, 8 species of n-6 PUFAs, 7 species of n-3 PUFAs).
Statistics
Given conditions tested with β = 0.8 and α = 0.05, at least 6 mice per group were required for the analysis, estimated by using G*Power 3.1
[62]
. We ensured this minimum sample size was reached for phenotypic and omics experiments, and n = 3–4 was achieved for validation experiments. All data are presented as mean ± SEM. For non-omics datasets, data normality (quantile-quantile plot) and variance (
F
-test) were evaluated followed by parametric tests (unpaired
t
-test or Welch's
t
-test) or non-parametric Mann-Whitney
U
test, unless described differently (Prism v9.0, GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Heatmaps were created via
https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus/
.

Introduction
Dysregulated lipid metabolism is a significant contributor to retinal disorders including age-related macular degeneration, retinopathy of prematurity, diabetic retinopathy, and inherited retinal disorders
[1]
. The retina is highly enriched in lipids. Lipids play a crucial role as key components of cellular and organelle membranes. Additionally, lipids and their metabolites serve as signaling molecules, influencing processes such as metabolism, inflammation, cell survival, and apoptosis. They also provide essential substrates for energy production. Disturbance in lipid homeostasis may cause cellular dysfunction and cell death. Targeting the restoration of lipid balance via dietary lipid supplementation or pharmacological activation of specific lipid metabolic pathways could present a novel approach to treat eye diseases. However, current knowledge of retinal lipid processing is limited. Gaining deeper insights into retinal lipid biology could help address the knowledge gap in lipid imbalance and enhance lipid-based treatments for retinal diseases.
Photoreceptors, which transform light to electrical signal, are highly metabolically active exhibiting the highest mitochondrial density of any cell type
[2]
,
[3]
,
[4]
. Genetic mutations in mitochondrial function can cause dysfunctional retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors
[5]
,
[6]
,
[7]
,
[8]
,
[9]
. Limited access to energy sources such as glucose and lipids results in photoreceptor disruption
[10]
,
[11]
,
[12]
,
[13]
. Modulating photoreceptor metabolic substrates might protect against photoreceptor loss
[14]
. Photoreceptors uptake glucose from support cells
[15]
. Glucose mainly undergoes glycolysis generating lactate, rather than being metabolized through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)
[4]
,
[15]
,
[16]
,
[17]
,
[18]
. Recently, lipids have been shown to be an energy source for retinal OXPHOS
[11]
. Fatty acid oxidation (FAO) occurs in mitochondria and peroxisomes. Peroxisomes oxidize very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs, ≥C22), which are not efficiently oxidized in mitochondria, as well as long-chain monocarboxylic and dicarboxylic fatty acids, branched-chain fatty acids, and bile acid intermediates
[19]
. Shorter-chain lipids from peroxisomes can further be broken down by mitochondria
[19]
,
[20]
. Furthermore, peroxisomes generate docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)
[19]
. Genetic peroxisomal disorders cause severe RPE, photoreceptor, and retinal ganglion cell loss, accompanied by retinal arteriolar attenuation
[21]
,
[22]
,
[23]
. Disturbed long-chain fatty acid (LCFA, C13-C21) oxidation in patients causes chorioretinopathy, abnormal electroretinograms (ERG), and visual impairment
[24]
. Mice with genetic mutation of peroxisomal proteins show retinal pathology as early as age 2 to 3 weeks with decreased ERG signals and decreased photoreceptor thickness
[25]
,
[26]
. Multifunctional protein 2 deficiency (MFP2, a central enzyme of peroxisomal β-oxidation) in the RPE causes lysosomal dysfunction and RPE degeneration at 3 weeks
[27]
. These observations suggest a crucial role of FAO in neural retinal health and the need to explore retinal lipid processing.
Studies investigating the effect of altered lipids/metabolites on eye manifestations in peroxisomal disorders are limited
[25]
,
[28]
,
[29]
. In a mouse model of peroxisomal FAO deficiency targeting the enzyme MFP2, retinal accumulation of saturated VLCFAs and ultra-long chains (≥C34) was reported
[26]
. The observed retinal degeneration in
Mfp2
knockout (KO) mice has been attributed to shortage of DHA
[29]
, the most abundant n-3 PUFA in the retina
[30]
, essential for retinal membrane fluidity, disc morphology, and phototransduction
[31]
,
[32]
,
[33]
. Of note, n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)-derived metabolites such as resolvins, neuroprotectins, hydroxydocosahexaenoic acid, and prostaglandin E3 exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects
[28]
. ACOX1 (acyl-coenzyme A oxidase 1, catalyzing the desaturation of acyl-CoAs to 2-
trans
-enoyl-CoAs) is the first and key enzyme in peroxisomal FAO rendering VLCFAs and LCFAs to shorter-chain fatty acids subsequently used for mitochondrial OXPHOS.
Acox1
mutation leads to pseudo-neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy, a rare neurodegenerative childhood disease, with early abnormal retinal function and pigmentary retinopathy
[34]
,
[35]
.
Acox1
deficiency causes vision loss in flies as well as humans
[36]
. Although
Acox1
KO mice were generated ∼ 30 years ago
[37]
, the retinal phenotype has not been reported. In this mouse model of impaired peroxisomal function, we examined the impact of peroxisomal FAO on neural retinal development utilizing multiple omics techniques. Additionally, we tested whether supplementing specific metabolites and lipids could mitigate retinal dysfunction caused by peroxisomal FAO deficiency.

Immunohistochemistry

[46]

[52]

Transmission electron microscopy
Transmission electron microscopy was conducted as previously outlined with slight modifications
[53]
. In brief, mouse eyeballs were fixed overnight in ice-cold 2.5 % glutaraldehyde, 1.25 % formaldehyde, and 0.03 % picric acid in 0.1 M sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 7.4). After washing with 0.1 M cacodylate buffer, the eyeballs were cut in half and osmicated in 1 % osmium tetroxide and 1.5 % potassium ferrocyanide for 3 h, followed by several washes in distilled H
2
O. Samples were then washed with maleate buffer and incubated with 1 % uranyl acetate in maleate buffer for 1 h and rinsed multiple times with maleate buffer (pH 5.2). Dehydration was carried out sequentially with a graded ethanol series (up to 100 %) at 4 °C, which was changed three times over the course of 1 h. The samples were then incubated in propylene oxide for 1 h. Subsequently, the samples were placed in a mixture of propylene oxide and TAAB resin (TAAB Laboratories Equipment Ltd, Berkshire, England) at a 1:1 ratio, including catalyst, and left overnight at 4 °C. The next day, the eyeballs were embedded in pure TAAB resin and polymerized at 60 °C for 48 h in an experimental oven. Resin blocks were gently trimmed and sectioned to a thickness of 80 nm using an Ultracut-S microtome (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany). The ultra-thin sections were placed onto formvar-carbon coated slot copper grids and stained with 0.2 % lead citrate. Processed samples were observed under a JEOL 1200x electron microscope (JEOL, Tokyo, Japan), and images were captured with an AMT 2k CCD camera (AMT, Boston, MA, USA) and stored as TIFF files.

Fatty acid profiling
Retinal samples from P30
Acox1
KO (n = 18; both retinas pooled) vs. WT mice (n = 17) were processed for total lipid extraction
[61]
. Retinas were weighed and homogenized by glass homogenizers with sequential addition of 1.75 mL 0.88 % potassium chloride, 2 mL methanol, and 4 mL chloroform. Heptadecanoic acid (17:0) served as internal standard. Total lipids were extracted overnight then methylated with methanolic boron trifluoride (100 °C, 1 h). Fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) were quantified with a gas chromatograph equipped with flame ionization detector (Varian, Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA). FAMEs were eluted on a DB-FFAP (30 m x 0.25 mm i.d. x 0.25 μm film thickness) column by set program at initial oven temperature of 50 °C for 1 min, following a ramp to 130 °C at a rate of 30 °C/min, 175 °C at 10 °C/min, 230 °C at 5 °C/min then held for 9.5 min, and a ramp to 240 °C at 5 °C/min for 11.13 min. Via peak comparison to internal standard, 31 fatty acid species were quantified (8 species of saturated and 8 species of monounsaturated fatty acids, 8 species of n-6 PUFAs, 7 species of n-3 PUFAs).

F
-test) were evaluated followed by parametric tests (unpaired
t
-test or Welch's
t
-test) or non-parametric Mann-Whitney
U

Results
Deficiency of peroxisomal FAO caused retinal degeneration in the mouse retina
To investigate the impact of peroxisomal FAO deficiency on the developing retina, we examined retinal function and thickness at P30 in
Acox1
KO vs. WT controls.
Acox1
KO mice displayed a statistically significant global reduction in the rod signaling pathway and a trend towards decreased cone signaling (
Fig. 1
B, C
). No differences were observed between male and female mice (data not shown). No significant impact on total retinal thickness was observed (
Fig. 1
D
). We found a qualitative reduction of immunofluorescence for rhodopsin (receptor for light and a rod photoreceptor marker) in photoreceptor nucleus layer (
Fig. 1
E
). Immunofluorescence for cone arrestin (cone photoreceptor marker) was comparable in
Acox1
KO and WT retinas (
Fig. 1
F
). Furthermore, we observed a statistically significant and marked reduction in expression of genes involved in phototransduction (
Rho
,
Gnat1
,
Pde6b
,
Pde6g
) in
Acox1
KO retinas (
Fig. 1
G
). Taken together, disrupted peroxisomal FAO resulted in impaired neural retinal development.

Acox1
KO vs. WT retinas. In total, 3,776 proteins characterized by ≥ 2 unique peptides were identified. Significant changes in abundance (p < 0.05; q < 0.20) were observed in 924 proteins in
Acox1
KO vs. WT retinas, with 448 proteins decreased and 476 proteins increased in abundance in
Acox1
KO retinas. ACOX1 was among the most significantly decreased proteins (p < 0.0001) (
Fig. 2
A, B
) as further confirmed via Western blot (
Fig. 2
C, D
). GO pathway analysis of proteins with significantly reduced abundance in
Acox1
KO retinas demonstrated a statistically significant decrease of the GO biological processes
glycolytic process
,
pyruvate metabolic process
,
mitochondrial ATP synthesis-coupled electron transport
, and
cellular respiration
, suggesting disturbed retinal mitochondrial metabolism. Proteins with significantly increased abundance in
Acox1
KO retinas exhibited statistically significant GO enrichment involved in FAO and mitochondrial transport (
Fig. 2
E,
Supplementary Fig. 1
), pointing to a potential adaptive response of increased FAO proteins compensating for
Acox1
deficiency.

Acox1

Discussion
Disturbed lipid homeostasis is associated with many retinal metabolic disorders, but underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. Our current work uncovered the crucial role of peroxisomal FAO in retinal maturation and the metabolic impacts of peroxisomal FAO deficiency on the developing retina. Loss of the key enzyme in peroxisomal FAO resulted in reduced neuroretinal function, disrupted proteome, metabolome, and fatty acid profile. Restoring metabolic balance could present an effective approach to promote retinal growth in conditions of peroxisomal FAO deficiency.
Peroxisomes are crucial for eye metabolism as genetic peroxisomal disorders cause loss of RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells x
[21]
,
[22]
,
[23]
,
[64]
. Limited work has been performed to uncover mechanisms underlying peroxisomal disease progression in the retina. Our
Acox1
global KO approach effectively targeted peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, as evidenced by the elevated C24:0/C22:0 ratio in
Acox1
KO retinas, indicating reduced peroxisomal FAO activity
[65]
.
Acox1
KO retinas displayed significantly reduced rod-mediated ERG signal and a trend towards decreased cone-mediated ERG signal, in line with the observed reduction of rhodopsin immunofluorescence signal and rod-specific
Rho
,
Gnat1
,
Pde6b
, and
Pde6g
transcripts. Clinically, some patients with peroxisomal disorders present with retinitis pigmentosa, affecting rods in the periphery first and only later followed by cones
[64]
, in line with our data. Flies with
Acox1
loss of function mutation exhibit a progressive ERG signal deterioration, and pharmacological interventions decreasing VLCFA synthesis reduce retinal neurodegeneration
[36]
. Mice with peroxisomal biogenesis factor 1 (
Pex1
) knock-in show retinal pathology at age 2 weeks with decreased ERG signal persisting until at least age 32 weeks
[25]
. Mice with MFP2 deficiency (a central enzyme of peroxisomal FAO) display decreased retinal and photoreceptor thickness
[26]
. In our study, retinal thickness was unaffected in
Acox1
KO retinas at 1 month of age. However, we found slightly decreased thickness of photoreceptor nuclear layer and significantly increased inner nuclear layer thickness at 5 months of age (data not shown). We speculate that the compensatory induction of peroxisomal and mitochondrial FAO proteins might attenuate the disruption of retinal structure. In patients with peroxisomal retinal disorders, clinical findings are not limited to retinal thinning, as some cases present with macular edema or schisis
[66]
.
Mfp2
KO mice also display reduced retinal DHA, and increased ARA at age 3 weeks
[26]

Our current work has several limitations. First, fatty acid profiling focused on targeted lipids with the advantage of measuring lipid concentrations. However, the impacts of
Acox1
deficiency on other lipids processed by peroxisomes remain unknown, especially those with > C24 carbon chain. Of note, VLC-PUFAs are essential for retinal function
[101]

[102]
, but the contribution of peroxisomal lipids/metabolites remains unknown. Last but not least, the impact of nutrient intervention at a longer term needs to be evaluated, especially when translating the approach into clinical application. Nevertheless, these future investigations hold the potential to unlock targeted nutritional approaches that may improve retinal health and function across different age groups and conditions.
Conclusion
Peroxisomal FAO is essential in retinal lipid processing and metabolic homeostasis of the developing retina. Our work highlights the benefits of restoring metabolic balance by supplementing depleted nutrients (lipids/metabolites) potentially serving as a general approach to treat retinal degenerative disorders.
